paragraphs.heading: What atomic physics studies
paragraphs.text: Atomic physics looks at the atom as an isolated system of its own: one nucleus with one or more electrons bound to it. Its main interest is how those electrons are arranged around the nucleus, and how those arrangements change. Ions count as atoms here too, unless someone says otherwise.

paragraphs.heading: Not the same as nuclear physics
paragraphs.text: In everyday English, "atomic" and "nuclear" are often used as if they meant the same thing, so the name can bring nuclear power and weapons to mind. Physicists keep the two apart. Atomic physics treats the atom as a nucleus plus electrons, while nuclear physics studies nuclear reactions and the special properties of the nucleus itself. In practice the border is blurry, and atomic physics is often grouped with molecular and optical physics.

paragraphs.heading: Why atoms can be taken alone
paragraphs.text: The field mostly studies atoms one at a time. It does not deal with how molecules form, or with atoms packed together in solids. Treating atoms alone may sound unrealistic. But in a gas or a plasma, the time between meetings of atoms is huge compared with the time the processes inside an atom take. So each atom can be handled as though it were alone, which it is for most of the time, and this is why atomic physics supplies the theory beneath plasma physics and atmospheric physics.

paragraphs.heading: Excitation and ionization
paragraphs.text: Electrons sit in notional shells around the nucleus, and an electron in a shell is said to be in a bound state. They are normally in a ground state, but they can take in energy from light (photons), from magnetic fields, or from a particle that crashes into them. The energy needed to pull an electron right out of its shell is called its binding energy. If the electron absorbs more than that, it escapes, the extra turns into kinetic energy, the energy of motion, and the atom is said to be ionized. If it absorbs less, it moves up to an excited state instead.

paragraphs.heading: Falling back down
paragraphs.text: After some time, an excited electron makes a jump, called a transition, down to a lower state, and a neutral atom sends out a photon carrying the energy difference. If an inner electron is knocked out of the atom, an electron from further out may drop in to fill the gap. That can release visible light or a characteristic X-ray. Or the energy can pass to another bound electron and set it free, which is called the Auger effect, and which lets one photon ionize an atom more than once. Light can only reach certain electron arrangements, under strict selection rules, but collisions face no such rules.

paragraphs.heading: From an old idea to spectral lines
paragraphs.text: The idea that matter is made of atoms appears in texts from the 6th to the 2nd century BC, such as those of Democritus and the Vaiśeṣika Sūtra of Kaṇāda. John Dalton later recast it in the modern sense, as the basic unit of a chemical element, and Dmitri Mendeleev's periodic system was another big advance. Atomic physics truly began with the discovery of spectral lines and attempts to explain them, with Joseph von Fraunhofer the best-known name. Work on these lines led to the Bohr model of the atom and to quantum mechanics, which also gave chemistry and spectroscopy a new theoretical footing.

paragraphs.heading: Faster progress since the war
paragraphs.text: Since the Second World War, both theory and experiment have moved ahead quickly. Better computers allow larger and more detailed models of atoms and of collisions between particles. Advances in accelerators, detectors, lasers and ways of making magnetic fields have helped experimenters in the same way.
